newsitem.title: CANADA: APEC ministers to push on financial services.
newsitem.headline: APEC ministers to push on financial services.

text.p: Trade ministers from the Asia Pacific region are ready to throw their support behind forging an agreement for free trade in financial services by the end of the year, Canada's trade minister said on Friday.

The financial services agreement has become a priority on the agenda for trade ministers at an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Montreal, Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton told reporters.
"I suspect that APEC can give it the final push," Eggleton said. "It will give it a push today and it will give it a push in November."

A senior U.S. official said the ministers also showed support for negotiating freer trade in environmental goods and services, medical equipment and natural resource products such as wood, paper and oil seeds.
The official said there was a lot of interest in accelerating talks on paper and wood products.

Canada is hosting the trade ministers' meeting and the APEC summit meeting this November in Vancouver, British Columbia. As host, Canada is under pressure to push the huge international organization toward concrete resolutions promoting free trade by November.

Last week, trade ministers from Canada, the United States, the European Union and Japan said at a so-called Quad meeting in Toronto that they would put forward requests for the financial services agreement by mid- June and offers no later than July 14. They aim to finalize a deal by December. But

the Quad leaders emphasized the need for Asia and Latin America to put together improved offers to the World Trade Organization. Last year, the United States pulled out of talks on financial services because of its disappointment in the offers from other countries.

The United States has said a deal must include provisions that allow firms to operate in other countries in the form of their choice. It must also allow full majority ownership and assure existing rights of foreign financial services providers.
Eggleton was optimistic on Friday that the Asia-Pacific region would be on his side.

"This is one area where we can demonstrate leadership and try and push the agenda forward, try to ensure that countries get in proposals by July ... and that we'll be able to reach a financial services agreement by the end of the year," Eggleton said.
The minister said he also expected to see support for expanding an agreement to liberalize information technology markets so that the deal will include more countries and more products.

Major trading powers have eyed China as a key new addition to the Information Technologies Agreement, which eliminates tariffs on various information technologies by 2000 for 39 countries. There has been some suggestion that for China to succeed with its bid to join the World Trade Organization it would have to sign the information technologies pact first. But when Eggleton was asked if China had shown any indication during APEC talks that it was willing to make concessions to comply with the agreement, Eggleton said no.
The trade ministers also expected to make progress on more transparent trade in mining, energy, power infrastructure, labor and telecommunications. The ministers added they were
advancing guidelines to cut customs red tape and streamline border regulations.
Canadian Revenue Minister Jane Stewart said she expected to have a blueprint on customs ready for the November summit.

Canadian trade officials said the APEC trade agenda was moving ahead much faster than leaders set out in guidelines two years ago. They said they expected the November summit would produce several named sectors targeted for liberalization.
"We have accelerated the pace," said one senior official. "Everyone is quite comfortable with it."

APEC includes Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
